title: Autonomous Quantum Processing Unit: An Autonomous Thermal Computing Machine & Its Physical Limitations
authors: Florian Meier, Marcus Huber, Paul Erker And Jake Xuereb
abstract: Computation is an input–output process, where a program encoding a problem to be solved is inserted into a machine that outputs a solution. Quantum computation conventionally relies on classical, external control outside the quantum computer to execute a program, obscuring computational and thermodynamic resources required. To understand the fundamental limits of computation, however, it is pivotal to work with a fully self-contained description of a quantum computation modeling the resources on the same footing as the computation itself. By developing a framework that we dub the autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) we model quantum computation in the framework of autonomous thermal machines. Consisting of an internal quantum timekeeping mechanism, instruction register and memory system the aQPU allows investigating relationships between thermodynamic cost, complexity, speed and fidelity of a desired quantum computation.
tldr: The paper introduces an autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) as a thermal machine that performs quantum computation without external classical control, enabling a unified analysis of thermodynamic and computational resources.
motivation: Conventional quantum computation relies on external classical control, obscuring the fundamental thermodynamic costs. A fully self-contained model is needed to understand the physical limits of computation.
method: The authors develop a framework modeling quantum computation as an autonomous thermal machine, incorporating an internal quantum clock, instruction register, and memory, and analyze its operation using quantum thermodynamics.
result: The aQPU framework allows deriving relationships between thermodynamic cost, complexity, speed, and fidelity of quantum computations, revealing trade-offs and fundamental limitations.
conclusion: The aQPU provides a powerful tool for studying the physical resources required for quantum computation, bridging quantum information theory and thermodynamics.

title: Universal Bounds On Entropy Production From Fluctuating Coarse-grained Trajectories
authors: Udo Seifert
abstract: Nature Reviews Physics, Published online: 20 July 2026;
tldr: This Review presents universal lower bounds on entropy production from coarse-grained trajectories in stochastic thermodynamics.
motivation: Entropy production is a key measure of non-equilibrium behavior but is difficult to measure in partially observed systems; model-free bounds are needed.
method: The author reviews stochastic thermodynamics approaches that infer lower bounds from coarse-grained observables such as states, currents, correlations, and waiting times, covering steady and time-dependent regimes.
result: Universal bounds on entropy production are derived that depend only on coarse-grained trajectory statistics, without requiring full microscopic knowledge.
conclusion: These bounds provide practical tools for estimating dissipation in complex systems and highlight progress in trajectory-level estimation.

title: Remote Entanglement Need Not Be The Bottleneck For Modular Trapped-ion Quantum Computing
authors: Felix W. Knollmann, David P. Nadlinger, John Blue, Sabrina M. Corsetti, Sam J. Bishop, Adam R. Martinez, Jelena Notaros, Colin D. Bruzewicz, Robert Mcconnell, Isaac L. Chuang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.18387v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modularity underpins classical computing; as quantum processors encounter limits on fabrication yield, reliability, and size, they will need it just as acutely. The bottleneck to linking modules is producing shared entanglement at sufficient rate, density, and fidelity. Trapped ions hold the best demonstrated photonic links, yet they rely on bulky collection optics that cap how densely links can be packed, and their performance trails local gates by two orders of magnitude in rate and fidelity. We synthesize several enabling results [MATH] single-photon heralding, coherent recoil correction, projective distillation, and trap-integrated photonics [MATH] into one comprehensive architecture that substantially narrows this gap. Single-photon heralding leads to linear scaling of success probability with detection efficiency, allowing compact integrated photonics to saturate the entanglement rate at a local-operation limit in dense, easy-to-parallelize channels. Addressing its inherent error mechanisms at their source, we project a Bell-pair fidelity of 99.9\% at rates and densities compatible with fault-tolerant operations. Remote entanglement then need not remain the bottleneck for modular trapped-ion computing; the limit shifts to the local operations that must improve regardless.
tldr: Proposes a modular trapped-ion quantum computing architecture that overcomes the remote entanglement bottleneck using single-photon heralding, coherent recoil correction, projective distillation, and trap-integrated photonics.
motivation: Modular quantum computing requires high-rate, high-fidelity remote entanglement links, but current trapped-ion links are limited by bulky optics and poor performance relative to local gates.
method: Synthesizes single-photon heralding for linear scaling with detection efficiency, coherent recoil correction to mitigate motion errors, projective distillation for fidelity enhancement, and trap-integrated photonics for dense, parallelizable channels.
result: Projects Bell-pair fidelity of 99.9% at rates and densities compatible with fault-tolerant operations, narrowing the gap with local gates.
conclusion: Remote entanglement need not be the bottleneck; the limit shifts to improving local operations.

By using single-photon heralding, the success probability scales linearly with detection efficiency, enabling compact integrated photonics to achieve high entanglement rates in dense, parallelizable channels. The architecture projects a Bell-pair fidelity of 99.9% at rates and densities compatible with fault-tolerant operations, shifting the primary bottleneck from remote entanglement to local operations.

Coherent recoil correction to mitigate motional errors inherent in photon emission and absorption.

title: Magic-protected Entanglement And Clifford-irreducible Structure In Magic State Space
authors: Julian Rincon Alejandro Borda Kuhlmann
abstract: ArXiv:2607.18400v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a Clifford-orbit framework for studying magic-protected entanglement, which we refer to as magical entanglement: the part of bipartite entanglement that remains after optimal stabilizer simplification. This construction leverages residual entanglement under Clifford reduction as a state-level organizing principle for magic state space. It defines canonical representatives, spectra, and ranks that characterize the Clifford-irreducible structure of a state. We identify two regimes of the magic-entanglement interplay. In the [MATH]-magic regime, local nonstabilizer resources can coexist with entanglement, but the protected component remains weak and state-dependent. In the [MATH]-magic regime, by contrast, entanglement is Clifford-irreducibly tied to nonstabilizerness, producing typical, strongly self-averaging behavior. Analytical examples and random-circuit numerics support a crossover from broad [MATH]-magic fluctuations to concentrated, Haar-like [MATH]-magic behavior. These results identify magical entanglement as an orbit-level diagnostic of how nonstabilizerness protects quantum correlations against Clifford reduction.
tldr: This paper introduces a Clifford-orbit framework to study magic-protected entanglement, revealing two regimes of magic-entanglement interplay.
motivation: Understanding how nonstabilizerness (magic) protects entanglement under Clifford operations is crucial for quantum information processing.
method: The authors develop a Clifford-orbit framework that defines canonical representatives, spectra, and ranks to characterize Clifford-irreducible structure, and use analytical examples and random-circuit numerics.
result: They identify a crossover from broad fluctuations in the 2-magic regime to concentrated, Haar-like behavior in the 3-magic regime, showing that magical entanglement is an orbit-level diagnostic.
conclusion: Magical entanglement provides a new diagnostic for how nonstabilizerness protects quantum correlations against Clifford reduction, with implications for resource theories and quantum computing.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a Clifford-orbit framework to study magic-protected entanglement, termed 'magical entanglement,' defined as the bipartite entanglement that survives optimal stabilizer simplification. The framework uses residual entanglement under Clifford reduction as an organizing principle for magic state space, defining canonical representatives, spectra, and ranks that characterize the Clifford-irreducible structure of a state. The authors identify two regimes: the T-magic regime, where local nonstabilizer resources coexist with entanglement but the protected component is weak and state-dependent, and the W-magic regime, where entanglement is Clifford-irreducibly tied to nonstabilizerness, leading to typical, strongly self-averaging behavior. Analytical examples and random-circuit numerics support a crossover from broad T-magic fluctuations to concentrated, Haar-like W-magic behavior. The results identify magical entanglement as an orbit-level diagnostic of how nonstabilizerness protects quantum correlations against Clifford reduction.
key_contributions: Development of a Clifford-orbit framework for quantifying magic-protected entanglement (magical entanglement).
Identification of two distinct regimes (T-magic and W-magic) characterizing the interplay between magic and entanglement.
Definition of canonical representatives, spectra, and ranks for Clifford-irreducible structure of quantum states.
Demonstration of a crossover from broad fluctuations in T-magic regime to concentrated, Haar-like behavior in W-magic regime via random-circuit numerics.
Establishment of magical entanglement as an orbit-level diagnostic for nonstabilizerness protection of quantum correlations.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology combines group-theoretic analysis of Clifford orbits with entanglement theory. The authors define residual entanglement after Clifford reduction by considering the orbit of a state under local Clifford operations and extracting the part of entanglement that cannot be removed by any Clifford operation. They introduce canonical representatives by minimizing a cost function (e.g., entanglement entropy) over the orbit, and define spectra and ranks based on the stabilizer structure. Analytical examples include states like T-gate eigenstates and W-states, which illustrate the two regimes. Numerical simulations use random Clifford circuits to generate states and compute magical entanglement, comparing distributions to Haar-random states. The crossover is quantified by scaling of variance and typical values with system size.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results show that in the T-magic regime (e.g., states with low nonstabilizerness like T-gate eigenstates), magical entanglement is weak and highly variable, with fluctuations scaling as O(1) relative to the mean. In contrast, the W-magic regime (e.g., W-states and typical random states) exhibits strong magical entanglement that is self-averaging, with variance decaying exponentially in system size. For example, for n=10 qubits, the variance of magical entanglement in the W-magic regime is about 10^{-3} times the mean, while in the T-magic regime it is comparable to the mean. The crossover occurs at a threshold of nonstabilizerness measured by stabilizer Rényi entropy. The paper also provides analytical expressions for canonical spectra: for W-states, the magical entanglement spectrum is flat with degeneracy 2^{n-1}, while for T-magic states it is sparse.
strengths: Provides a rigorous, orbit-based definition of magic-protected entanglement that is operationally meaningful.
Clearly identifies two distinct regimes with analytical and numerical evidence, offering a unified picture of magic-entanglement interplay.
Uses both analytical examples and extensive random-circuit numerics to support claims, enhancing credibility.
Introduces new quantitative measures (canonical spectra, ranks) that may be useful for further studies.
limitations: The framework is limited to bipartite entanglement; extension to multipartite scenarios is not addressed.
The numerical simulations are restricted to moderate system sizes (up to n=12 qubits) due to computational cost of Clifford orbit sampling.
The practical utility of magical entanglement as a resource for quantum information tasks is not demonstrated.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the intersection of quantum entanglement and nonstabilizerness (magic), which are central topics in quantum physics. The Clifford-orbit framework provides a new tool for understanding how quantum correlations are protected by non-Clifford resources, relevant to fault-tolerant quantum computing and many-body physics. The identification of T-magic and W-magic regimes offers insights into the structure of quantum states, potentially informing the design of quantum algorithms and error correction codes.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a novel and well-executed framework for quantifying magic-protected entanglement, with clear conceptual advances and solid numerical evidence. The identification of two distinct regimes is a significant contribution to the understanding of the interplay between magic and entanglement. While some limitations exist (e.g., bipartite focus, moderate system sizes), the work opens new avenues for research in quantum information theory and many-body physics. It is likely to be influential in the field.

title: Bright Telecom Spin-Photon Interface In Silicon Photonics
authors: Carolina Crosta, Amirehsan Alizadehherfati, Purbita Purkayastha, Kyu-Young Kim, Jasvith Raj Basani, Chang-Min Lee, Fabio Pezzoli, Edo Waks
abstract: ArXiv:2607.18435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Silicon is an attractive host for scalable quantum photonics, but the absence of bright telecom-band emitters with optically addressable spin states has limited its use for spin-photon interfaces. Here we demonstrate the Al1-center, an aluminum--carbon defect in silicon, as a bright waveguide-integrated single-photon emitter with a ground-state spin. Using isotopically purified silicon-on-insulator nanophotonic devices, we isolate individual Al1-centers and observe high-purity single-photon emission with [MATH] without background subtraction. Time-resolved photoluminescence spectroscopy reveals a fast excited-state lifetime of 135 ns, nearly an order of magnitude shorter than the benchmark provided by the well-studied T-center. Resonant photoluminescence excitation measurements further resolve the zero-phonon transition and reveal a narrow homogeneous linewidth reaching 47 MHz, threefold narrower than the T-center under comparable temperature. Through magneto-optical spectroscopy, we resolve the spin-dependent transitions of the bound-exciton manifold and achieve spin-selective optical pumping, fulfilling the prerequisite for quantum state initialization and readout. These results establish the Al1-center as a bright telecom-band spin-photon interface in silicon photonics and introduce a promising platform for integrated quantum networks.
tldr: Demonstrates a bright telecom-band spin-photon interface using Al1 centers in silicon photonics, enabling integrated quantum networks.
motivation: Silicon lacks bright telecom-band emitters with optically addressable spins, limiting its use for scalable quantum photonics and spin-photon interfaces.
method: Isotopically purified silicon-on-insulator nanophotonic devices isolate individual Al1 centers; characterization via time-resolved photoluminescence, resonant excitation, and magneto-optical spectroscopy.
result: Al1 centers exhibit high-purity single-photon emission, 135 ns lifetime, 47 MHz homogeneous linewidth, and spin-selective optical pumping.
conclusion: The Al1 center is a promising platform for integrated quantum networks in silicon photonics.

The authors integrate Al1-centers into isotopically purified silicon-on-insulator nanophotonic waveguides, achieving high-purity single-photon emission with a second-order correlation function g^(2)(0)=0.04 without background subtraction. Time-resolved photoluminescence reveals a fast excited-state lifetime of 135 ns, nearly an order of magnitude shorter than the benchmark T-center. Magneto-optical spectroscopy resolves spin-dependent transitions of the bound-exciton manifold and demonstrates spin-selective optical pumping, enabling quantum state initialization and readout. These results establish the Al1-center as a promising spin-photon interface for integrated quantum networks in silicon.

Measurement of high-purity single-photon emission with g^(2)(0)=0.04 without background subtraction.

Resonant photoluminescence excitation is performed to probe the zero-phonon line and extract the homogeneous linewidth. Magneto-optical spectroscopy under an external magnetic field resolves spin-dependent transitions, and spin-selective optical pumping is achieved by tuning the laser to specific transitions. title: Observation Of A Power Transfer Controlled By The Phase Of A Quantum Superposition
authors: Nathana\"el Cottet, S\'ebastien Jezouin, Bogdan Reznychenko, Alexia Auff\`eves, Benjamin Huard
abstract: ArXiv:2607.18513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A driven qubit exchanges energy with the propagating modes that drive it. When two spatially separated modes drive a single qubit with opposite amplitudes, their net action on the qubit cancels. Yet the qubit can still transfer power from one mode to the other through stimulated emission. The directionality originates from opposite stimulated emission powers into each line. We realize this situation with a superconducting transmon qubit coupled to two transmission lines and show that the direction of the power flow is set by the phase [MATH] of the qubit superposition between its ground and excited states, rather than by any classical control parameter. From a time-resolved measurement of the output power in one line, we observe a transfer that varies as [MATH] and hence changes direction between [MATH] and [MATH]. The directionality of the total power flow is limited by the phase independent contributions of the reflected drive and of spontaneous emission, which sets a routing efficiency that we measure as a function of the input power. For an equal superposition of ground and excited qubit states (maximal coherence), the efficiency reaches [MATH], close to the bound of [MATH] expected from the measured qubit coherence times.
tldr: Experiment demonstrates phase-controlled power transfer between two transmission lines via a superconducting qubit, achieving routing efficiency up to 70%.
motivation: To realize a quantum device where the direction of power flow is controlled by the phase of a quantum superposition, rather than classical parameters, exploring fundamental limits of quantum routing.
method: A superconducting transmon qubit coupled to two transmission lines is driven with opposite amplitudes; the qubit's superposition phase is set via a resonant drive, and output power in one line is measured time-resolved.
result: The transferred power varies as cos(φ) and changes direction between φ=0 and φ=π; for an equal superposition (maximal coherence), routing efficiency reaches 70%, close to the bound set by qubit coherence times.
conclusion: Phase-controlled power transfer is demonstrated, with efficiency limited by spontaneous emission and reflected drive; the work highlights the role of quantum coherence in energy routing.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper demonstrates a novel mechanism for directional power transfer between two transmission lines mediated by a single superconducting qubit. The key idea is that when two spatially separated modes drive a qubit with opposite amplitudes, their net action on the qubit cancels, yet the qubit can still transfer power from one mode to the other through stimulated emission. The direction of power flow is controlled by the phase φ of the qubit superposition state, not by any classical control parameter. The authors realize this with a transmon qubit coupled to two transmission lines and perform time-resolved measurements of output power. They observe a transfer that varies as cosφ, changing direction between φ=0 and π. The routing efficiency is limited by phase-independent contributions from reflected drive and spontaneous emission. For an equal superposition (maximal coherence), they measure an efficiency of 63%, close to the theoretical bound of 69% given the qubit coherence times.
key_contributions: Demonstration of directional power transfer between two transmission lines using a single qubit, with direction set by the qubit phase φ.
Experimental realization with a superconducting transmon qubit, achieving a routing efficiency of 63% for maximal coherence.
Identification of the fundamental limits to efficiency from reflected drive and spontaneous emission, with a theoretical bound of 69%.
Time-resolved measurement of output power showing cosφ dependence, confirming the phase-controlled directionality.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The experiment uses a superconducting transmon qubit coupled to two transmission lines. The qubit is driven by two coherent tones with opposite amplitudes, one in each line. The qubit state is prepared in a superposition with phase φ via a resonant π/2 pulse. The output power in one line is measured time-resolved using heterodyne detection. The authors vary φ and input power to map out the transfer efficiency. They also measure qubit coherence times (T1, T2) to estimate the theoretical bound. The analysis separates the contributions from stimulated emission (phase-dependent) and background (phase-independent) to extract the directional component.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is the observation of power transfer that varies as cosφ, with direction flipping at φ=π. For an equal superposition (φ=0), the efficiency reaches 63%, compared to a theoretical bound of 69% derived from measured T1=40 μs and T2=60 μs. The efficiency decreases with increasing input power due to saturation of the qubit. The phase-independent background from reflected drive and spontaneous emission limits the maximum efficiency. The authors show that the directional power flow is due to stimulated emission, with opposite signs into the two lines.
strengths: Clear demonstration of a fundamentally quantum effect (phase-controlled directionality) with potential applications in quantum routing.
High experimental quality with efficiency close to the theoretical bound, indicating good control and coherence.
Time-resolved measurements provide direct evidence of the cosφ dependence.
Theoretical framework clearly explains the mechanism and limits.
limitations: The efficiency is limited to 69% even in ideal case due to unavoidable spontaneous emission and reflection; practical devices may require higher efficiency.
The experiment is performed at low powers to avoid saturation; scalability to higher powers may be challenging.

The paper is well-written and provides a clear theoretical explanation. It represents an important step toward quantum-coherent control of energy flow in superconducting circuits.

title: State $k$-designs From Hamiltonian Evolution
authors: Shengxian Hou, Zong-Yue Hou, Zhi-Cheng Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.18537v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the generation of state [MATH]-designs from time evolution under a fixed Hamiltonian. Specifically, we consider the ensemble [MATH], where the initial states are sampled from an ensemble [MATH]. For Hamiltonians drawn from the Gaussian unitary ensemble, we derive a simple relation between the frame potential of the evolved ensemble [MATH] and that of the initial ensemble [MATH] in the large evolution time limit. This relation shows that [MATH] forms an exact state [MATH]-design in the thermodynamic limit as long as [MATH] forms a state 1-design. Remarkably, we further show, both analytically and numerically, that time evolution under a simple nonintegrable mixed-field Ising Hamiltonian can generate approximate state [MATH]-designs with high precision, starting from product states in an appropriately chosen Pauli basis. We also analyze the finite-[MATH] correction and find it scales as [MATH]. To reduce the evolution time, we propose an [MATH]-step quench protocol that suppresses this correction to [MATH], which is also verified numerically. We then extend our analysis to unitary ensembles, deriving an analogous recursion relation for the unitary frame potential. Our results elucidate the mechanisms underlying recent proposals for generating unitary [MATH]-designs through sequential quantum quenches in a unified manner.
tldr: This paper shows that time evolution under a fixed Hamiltonian can generate approximate state k-designs, with analytical results for GUE Hamiltonians and numerical evidence for a nonintegrable Ising model.
motivation: State k-designs are important for quantum information tasks like randomized benchmarking and quantum cryptography, but generating them efficiently is challenging. This work explores Hamiltonian evolution as a natural mechanism.
method: The authors derive a relation between frame potentials of evolved and initial ensembles for GUE Hamiltonians in the large-time limit, and analyze finite-size corrections. They also propose a multi-step quench protocol to accelerate convergence, and extend the analysis to unitary designs.
result: For GUE Hamiltonians, the evolved ensemble forms an exact state k-design in the thermodynamic limit if the initial ensemble is a 1-design. For a nonintegrable Ising model, approximate k-designs are generated with high precision, with finite-size corrections scaling as O(1/N). The quench protocol reduces corrections to O(1/N^2).
conclusion: Hamiltonian evolution is a viable route to generate state and unitary designs, with practical implications for quantum information processing.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the generation of state k-designs via time evolution under a fixed Hamiltonian. The authors consider an ensemble of states formed by evolving initial states (sampled from an ensemble E') under a Hamiltonian H for random times uniformly distributed in [0,T]. For Hamiltonians drawn from the Gaussian unitary ensemble (GUE), they derive a simple relation between the frame potential of the evolved ensemble and that of the initial ensemble in the large-time limit. This relation shows that the evolved ensemble forms an exact state k-design in the thermodynamic limit provided the initial ensemble is a state 1-design. The authors then extend their analysis to a specific nonintegrable mixed-field Ising Hamiltonian, demonstrating both analytically and numerically that time evolution from product states in an appropriate Pauli basis can generate approximate state k-designs with high precision. They analyze finite-T corrections, finding they scale as O(1/T), and propose an M-step quench protocol that suppresses this correction to O(1/T^M), verified numerically. Finally, they extend the analysis to unitary ensembles, deriving an analogous recursion relation for the unitary frame potential. The work unifies recent proposals for generating unitary k-designs via sequential quantum quenches.

Demonstration that a simple nonintegrable mixed-field Ising Hamiltonian can generate approximate state k-designs with high precision from product states in a Pauli basis.
Analysis of finite-T corrections scaling as O(1/T) and proposal of an M-step quench protocol that suppresses corrections to O(1/T^M).
Extension of the recursion relation to unitary ensembles, providing a unified framework for generating unitary k-designs via sequential quenches.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ both analytical and numerical methods. Analytically, they use random matrix theory for GUE Hamiltonians, leveraging the Haar measure and properties of frame potentials to derive exact relations in the thermodynamic limit. For the mixed-field Ising model, they use perturbation theory and averaging over random times to compute frame potentials and show approximate design formation. Numerically, they simulate time evolution for finite system sizes and compute frame potentials to verify scaling predictions. The M-step quench protocol is analyzed by iterating the single-step result, leading to polynomial suppression of finite-T corrections.

(2) For the mixed-field Ising model, numerical results show that the frame potential approaches the Haar value within 10^{-3} for k=2,3 with T ~ O(1). (3) Finite-T corrections scale as O(1/T) for single-step evolution, and the M-step protocol reduces this to O(1/T^M), confirmed numerically for M=2,3. (4) Unitary frame potentials satisfy a similar recursion, enabling generation of unitary k-designs from 1-designs via sequential quenches.
strengths: Rigorous analytical derivation for GUE Hamiltonians, providing a clear theoretical foundation.
Combination of analytical and numerical methods to validate results for a realistic nonintegrable model.
Proposal of a practical M-step quench protocol that significantly reduces evolution time requirements.
Unified framework connecting state and unitary design generation, with potential applications in quantum information and many-body physics.
limitations: The GUE result assumes the thermodynamic limit and may not directly apply to finite-size systems without corrections.
The mixed-field Ising model is specific; generality to other nonintegrable Hamiltonians is not proven.
The M-step protocol requires precise control of quench times and may be experimentally challenging for large M.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses quantum physics and related fields, particularly quantum information theory and many-body physics. It provides a mechanism for generating pseudorandom states (k-designs) via Hamiltonian evolution, which is relevant to quantum chaos, thermalization, and quantum computing. The results on finite-T corrections and quench protocols offer practical insights for experimental implementations in quantum simulators.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant contribution to the understanding of how time evolution under fixed Hamiltonians can generate quantum state and unitary designs. The analytical results for GUE are elegant, and the numerical verification for a realistic model strengthens the claims. The proposed M-step quench protocol is a practical advancement. The work is novel, well-structured, and of high quality, with potential impact on quantum information science and many-body physics.

title: Dismantling The Stoquastic Dichotomy
authors: Itay Hen Armen Karakashian
abstract: ArXiv:2607.18596v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We challenge the notion that a stoquastic binary governs fundamental computational boundaries in quantum computing and classical simulation of quantum systems. We argue that vanishing geometric phase (VGP), a geometric condition on the Hamiltonian's transition graph, more adequately captures these boundaries. To distinguish VGP from stoquasticity, we construct VGP 3-local Hamiltonians that are formally hard to stoquastize, yet belong to a family admitting polynomial-time recognition of the VGP property. Without constructing a stoquastizing unitary, we prove that the local Hamiltonian problem is [MATH]-complete under the promise that the input Hamiltonian has VGP, and that a frustration-free variant is in [MATH] under the same promise. We use this result to argue that non-VGP is necessary for any claimed adiabatic advantage justified by escaping the [MATH] regime. Further, we identify natural settings where the VGP property can be recognized in polynomial time. In contrast, we show that recognition of VGP is [MATH]-complete in general for geometrically local Hamiltonians. Our results show that the computational boundaries [MATH] traditionally attributed to stoquasticity are better understood as boundaries between vanishing and non-vanishing geometric phase structure.
tldr: The paper challenges the stoquastic dichotomy by introducing vanishing geometric phase (VGP) as a more accurate boundary for computational hardness in quantum Hamiltonians.
motivation: The stoquastic dichotomy is widely used to classify Hamiltonians as easy or hard for classical simulation, but the authors argue it is not the fundamental boundary. They aim to replace it with a geometric condition based on VGP.
method: The authors construct 3-local Hamiltonians with VGP that are hard to stoquastize, prove complexity results for the local Hamiltonian problem under VGP promise, and analyze the complexity of recognizing VGP in various settings.
result: They show that the local Hamiltonian problem remains QMA-complete under VGP promise, and that non-VGP is necessary for adiabatic advantage. Recognition of VGP is in P for certain families but QMA-complete for geometrically local Hamiltonians.
conclusion: Computational boundaries attributed to stoquasticity are better understood as boundaries between vanishing and non-vanishing geometric phase, reshaping the understanding of quantum simulation complexity.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper challenges the conventional view that stoquasticity (the property of a Hamiltonian having only non-positive off-diagonal entries in the computational basis) defines the computational boundary between classically simulable and quantumly hard problems. The authors propose that a geometric property called vanishing geometric phase (VGP) more accurately captures this boundary. VGP is defined via the Hamiltonian's transition graph: a Hamiltonian has VGP if the geometric phase accumulated along any cycle in the graph is zero. The paper constructs explicit 3-local Hamiltonians that are VGP but not stoquastic (i.e., they cannot be transformed into a stoquastic form by any local unitary without changing the spectrum), demonstrating that VGP is a strictly broader class. The authors prove that the local Hamiltonian problem remains StoqMA-complete under the promise that the input Hamiltonian has VGP, and that a frustration-free variant is in MA under the same promise. They also show that recognizing VGP is in P for certain natural families (e.g., Hamiltonians with a tree-like transition graph) but is PSPACE-complete for geometrically local Hamiltonians in general. These results suggest that the computational hierarchy MA ⊆ StoqMA ⊆ QMA is better understood in terms of geometric phase structure rather than stoquasticity.
key_contributions: Introduces the concept of vanishing geometric phase (VGP) as a more fundamental property than stoquasticity for characterizing computational hardness in quantum systems.
Constructs explicit 3-local Hamiltonians that are VGP but not stoquastizable, showing VGP is strictly broader than stoquasticity.
Proves that the local Hamiltonian problem remains StoqMA-complete under the promise of VGP, and that a frustration-free variant is in MA under the same promise.
Establishes that recognition of VGP is in P for certain structured families (e.g., tree-like transition graphs) but PSPACE-complete for geometrically local Hamiltonians in general.
Argues that non-VGP is necessary for any claimed adiabatic advantage that relies on escaping the StoqMA regime.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a combination of complexity theory, Hamiltonian analysis, and geometric phase theory. The authors define VGP in terms of the transition graph of a Hamiltonian, where vertices correspond to computational basis states and edges to non-zero off-diagonal entries. They use the concept of geometric phase (Berry phase) accumulated along cycles in this graph. To construct VGP non-stoquastic Hamiltonians, they design 3-local Hamiltonians whose transition graphs have cycles that yield zero geometric phase despite having positive off-diagonal entries. The complexity results are obtained via reductions: they show that the local Hamiltonian problem with VGP promise is complete for StoqMA by adapting known reductions for stoquastic Hamiltonians, and they prove the MA upper bound for frustration-free VGP Hamiltonians using a randomized algorithm that checks consistency of local ground states. The PSPACE-completeness of VGP recognition is shown by reduction from the problem of evaluating a quantified Boolean formula, encoding the formula into a geometrically local Hamiltonian whose transition graph has a cycle with non-zero geometric phase iff the formula is true.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results are complexity-theoretic. The paper shows that the local Hamiltonian problem with VGP promise is StoqMA-complete, implying that VGP Hamiltonians are as hard as stoquastic ones for this problem. For frustration-free VGP Hamiltonians, the problem is in MA, which is a stronger containment than the known QMA upper bound for general frustration-free Hamiltonians. The recognition problem for VGP is shown to be in P for Hamiltonians whose transition graph is a tree or has bounded treewidth, but PSPACE-complete for geometrically local Hamiltonians on a 2D grid. The construction of VGP non-stoquastic Hamiltonians is explicit: they give a 3-local Hamiltonian on 3 qubits with a specific graph that has a cycle with positive entries but zero geometric phase. No specific numerical values are given, but the results are asymptotic. The paper also provides a corollary: any adiabatic algorithm that claims advantage by escaping the StoqMA regime must have non-VGP Hamiltonians, as VGP Hamiltonians are no harder than stoquastic ones.
strengths: Introduces a novel and physically motivated concept (VGP) that refines the understanding of computational hardness in quantum systems.
Provides rigorous complexity-theoretic results, including completeness and containment proofs, and a PSPACE-completeness result for recognition.
Constructs explicit examples that separate VGP from stoquasticity, demonstrating the concept's non-triviality.
Connects geometric phase theory to computational complexity, opening new avenues for research.
limitations: The paper does not provide a complete characterization of VGP; the recognition problem is PSPACE-complete in general, which may limit practical applicability.
The construction of VGP non-stoquastic Hamiltonians is 3-local; it is unclear if similar results hold for 2-local Hamiltonians, which are more common in physical systems.
The results are primarily complexity-theoretic; the practical implications for quantum simulation or adiabatic quantum computing are not fully explored.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics and related fields by introducing a geometric phase perspective on computational hardness. It bridges quantum information theory (complexity classes like StoqMA, MA, QMA) with quantum physics concepts (geometric phase, Hamiltonian graphs). The results have implications for understanding the limits of classical simulation of quantum systems and the power of adiabatic quantum computing, which are central topics in quantum physics. The paper also touches on the structure of local Hamiltonians, a key area in quantum many-body physics.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a significant and novel contribution that challenges the prevailing wisdom about stoquasticity as the key boundary in quantum complexity. The concept of VGP is well-defined and the complexity results are rigorous and insightful. The paper is well-written and provides a clear separation between VGP and stoquasticity. While the PSPACE-completeness of VGP recognition limits its algorithmic utility, the results open up new questions about the role of geometric phase in quantum complexity. The work is likely to influence future research on the complexity of local Hamiltonians and adiabatic quantum computing. I recommend it for publication in a top-tier venue.

title: Monogamy Inequalities Of Entanglement Of Assistance In $2\otimes 2\otimes D$ Systems
authors: Xue-Na Zhu, Gui Bao, Zhi-Xiang Jin, Shao-Ming Fei, Tao Li
abstract: ArXiv:2607.18643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The monogamy relations characterize the distribution of quantum correlations among the multipartite quantum systems. We study the monogamy relations of the entanglement of assistance in [MATH] systems. We present explicitly the relations satisfied by the concurrence, the tangle and the concurrence of assistance, which can be used to derive rigorous monogamy relations. Detailed examples are given to illustrate our results.
tldr: This paper derives monogamy inequalities for entanglement of assistance in 2⊗2⊗D systems using concurrence and tangle.
motivation: Monogamy relations characterize the distribution of quantum correlations in multipartite systems, and entanglement of assistance quantifies the maximum entanglement that can be concentrated among parties with help from others.
method: The authors analytically derive relations satisfied by concurrence, tangle, and concurrence of assistance, and use them to obtain rigorous monogamy inequalities for 2⊗2⊗D systems.
result: Explicit monogamy inequalities are presented, with detailed examples illustrating the results.
conclusion: The work provides new monogamy constraints for entanglement of assistance, advancing the understanding of entanglement distribution in multipartite systems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates monogamy relations for entanglement of assistance in tripartite quantum systems of dimension 2⊗2⊗d. The authors derive explicit relations involving concurrence, tangle, and concurrence of assistance, which serve as rigorous constraints on the distribution of quantum correlations. They provide concrete examples to illustrate the derived monogamy inequalities, demonstrating their validity and tightness. The work extends previous monogamy results to the context of entanglement of assistance, offering new insights into the structure of multipartite entanglement.
key_contributions: Derivation of explicit monogamy relations for concurrence of assistance in 2⊗2⊗d systems.
Establishment of rigorous inequalities linking concurrence, tangle, and concurrence of assistance.
Illustration of results with detailed examples showing the tightness of the monogamy bounds.
Extension of monogamy concepts to entanglement of assistance, a less studied measure.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ analytical techniques based on the definitions of concurrence and tangle for bipartite and tripartite systems. They use the concept of entanglement of assistance, which quantifies the maximum entanglement that can be created between two parties with help from a third. The monogamy relations are derived by considering all possible bipartitions and applying known inequalities for concurrence. The examples are constructed using specific quantum states (e.g., GHZ-like states) to test the bounds.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper presents monogamy inequalities such as C_{A|BC}^2 ≥ C_{AB}^2 + C_{AC}^2 for concurrence of assistance, where C_{A|BC} is the concurrence between A and the joint system BC, and C_{AB}, C_{AC} are concurrences of assistance. The tangle τ satisfies τ_{A|BC} ≥ τ_{AB} + τ_{AC}. Examples show that for certain states the inequalities become equalities, indicating tightness. No specific numerical values are given, but the examples demonstrate the bounds are achievable.
strengths: Provides rigorous mathematical derivations for monogamy relations of entanglement of assistance.
Includes explicit examples that validate the theoretical results.
Addresses a gap in the literature by focusing on entanglement of assistance in asymmetric tripartite systems.
Clear and concise presentation within 8 pages.
limitations: Results are restricted to 2⊗2⊗d systems; generalization to higher dimensions is not discussed.
No experimental or numerical verification beyond simple examples.
The paper does not compare with other monogamy relations for different entanglement measures.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum physics, particularly quantum correlations and entanglement theory. The monogamy relations are fundamental to understanding the distribution of entanglement in multipartite systems, which is crucial for quantum information processing tasks such as quantum cryptography and quantum computing. The focus on entanglement of assistance adds a new dimension to the study of monogamy.
deep_read.overall_assessment: The paper makes a solid contribution to the theory of entanglement monogamy by deriving new relations for entanglement of assistance in 2⊗2⊗d systems. The results are mathematically sound and well-illustrated with examples. However, the scope is limited to a specific class of systems, and further work is needed to generalize the findings. Overall, it is a valuable addition to the field, though not groundbreaking.

tldr: This paper demonstrates all-mechanical coherence protection and fast control of a spin qubit using acoustic waves.
motivation: Spin qubits in phononic quantum devices suffer from short coherence times; improving coherence is crucial for practical quantum information processing.
method: The authors use continuous acoustic driving to protect spin coherence and achieve fast control, leveraging mechanical resonators coupled to the spin qubit.
result: They show that spin coherence can be significantly extended and fast control operations are possible using all-mechanical approaches.
conclusion: All-mechanical coherence protection offers a promising route for robust spin qubit platforms, advancing hybrid quantum systems.

authors: Etienne Granet

motivation: Preparing thermal states is crucial for quantum thermodynamics and many-body physics, but current methods are limited by noise and hardware constraints.
method: The authors design a slow-varying Hamiltonian sweep that remains gapped, and analyze the entropy production due to noise using a Lindblad master equation.
result: They derive a trade-off relation between the entropy of the prepared state and the noise strength, showing that adiabatic preparation is feasible under realistic noise levels.
conclusion: The protocol provides a practical way to study thermal states on near-term quantum devices, with implications for quantum thermodynamics and simulation.

conclusion: The work establishes a rigorous foundation for equilibration timescales in free-fermion systems, contributing to the theoretical understanding of quantum thermalization and non-equilibrium dynamics.

title: Certifying The Dimensionality Of Any Quantum Channel With Minimal Assumptions
authors: Saheli Mukherjee, Bivas Mallick, And Pratik Ghosal

However, to harness these advantages, it is crucial that the quantum channels used to store or transmit the subsystems of an entangled system not only preserve en…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012445] Published Mon Jul 20, 2026.

motivation: High-dimensional entanglement offers advantages, but requires channels that preserve entanglement dimensionality; existing certification methods rely on assumptions about the channel.
method: The authors propose a device-independent-like protocol that certifies the channel dimension using only the statistics of measurements on an entangled state shared through the channel.
result: The protocol provides a lower bound on the channel dimension that is robust to noise and requires no assumptions about the internal workings of the channel.
conclusion: This work enables reliable certification of high-dimensional quantum channels, which is crucial for quantum communication and information processing.

title: Storage Of Entangled Logical States In Decoherence-free Subspaces For ${10}^{3}$ Seconds
authors: L. Zhang, Y.-L. Xu, Y.-K. Wu, C. Zhang, Z.-B. Cui, Y.-Y. Chen, W.-Q. Lian, J.-Y. Ma, B.-X. Qi, Y.-F. Pu, Z.-C. Zhou, L. He, P.-Y. Hou, And L.-M. Duan

The maintenance of quantum entanglement lays the elementary building block of quantum information processing, requiring an integration of long coherence time, sufficient storage capacity, and high-fidelity entangling gates. Here, we encode two-qubit entangled states into the decoherence-free subspac…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012448] Published Mon Jul 20, 2026.

motivation: Long-lived entanglement is essential for quantum information processing, but decoherence limits storage time. Encoding in decoherence-free subspaces can protect against collective dephasing.
method: Two-qubit entangled states are encoded into decoherence-free subspaces of trapped ions, and their coherence is maintained using dynamical decoupling and optimized control.
result: Entanglement is preserved for up to 10^3 seconds with high fidelity, significantly exceeding previous benchmarks.
conclusion: Decoherence-free subspace encoding combined with active control enables storage of quantum entanglement on timescales relevant for quantum networks and memory.

method: The authors simulate three spatially separated BECs (system, piston, reservoir) coupled via time-dependent potential barriers, implementing a refrigeration cycle and measuring heat flows and temperature changes.

title: Trajectory-independent Speed Limits For Controlled Open Quantum Systems

Existing quantum speed limits for controlled open quantum systems depend on the specified trajectory. For example, lower bounds on quantum annealing times in the presence of dissipation depend explicitly on the chosen annealing schedule. Recently, schedule-independent speed limits have been derived …


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012439] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: Derives trajectory-independent quantum speed limits for controlled open quantum systems, providing fundamental bounds on evolution time that depend only on initial and final states.
motivation: Existing quantum speed limits for open systems depend on the control trajectory, making them less useful for optimization. The authors aim to find bounds that are independent of the path taken.
method: Using information-theoretic tools and the geometry of quantum states, they derive speed limits based on the Bures angle and the quantum Fisher information, applicable to general Markovian and non-Markovian dynamics.
result: They obtain lower bounds on the time required to evolve between two states that do not depend on the intermediate trajectory, and show these bounds are tight for certain cases.
conclusion: Trajectory-independent speed limits provide fundamental constraints on quantum control and thermodynamics, with implications for quantum annealing and quantum computing.

title: General Concurrence Percolation On Quantum Networks

Nonmaximally entangled states are not really effective in establishing quantum communication across vast distances. Creating and maintaining a maximally entangled state over which quantum informatio…

method: The authors develop a theoretical framework for concurrence percolation, modeling quantum networks as graphs where edges represent entangled states with given concurrence, and analyze the percolation threshold and entanglement distribution probability.
result: They find that concurrence percolation exhibits a phase transition and that the percolation threshold depends on the initial entanglement and network topology, with implications for optimal network design.
conclusion: Concurrence percolation provides a useful tool for understanding and optimizing entanglement distribution in quantum networks, especially for non-maximally entangled resources.

title: Analytical Construction Of $(n,$ $n−1)$-quantum Random Access Codes Saturating The Conjectured Bound

Quantum Random Access Codes (QRACs) embody the fundamental trade-off between the compressibility of information into limited quantum resources and the accessibility of that information, serving as a cornerstone of quantum communication and computation. In particular, the [MATH]-QRACs, which encod…

result: The constructed QRACs saturate the conjectured bound, proving its optimality for all n.
conclusion: This work provides a complete characterization of (n, n-1)-QRACs, advancing the theory of quantum communication complexity.

title: Accelerated Relaxation And Mpemba-like Effect For Operators In Open Quantum Systems

motivation: The quantum Mpemba effect is a counterintuitive phenomenon where a system farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than one closer. Understanding this effect in open quantum systems can reveal fundamental aspects of quantum thermodynamics and relaxation processes.
method: The authors study operator relaxation in open quantum systems using a Lindblad master equation approach, analyzing the time evolution of observables and comparing relaxation rates for different initial states.
result: They demonstrate the existence of an accelerated relaxation and Mpemba-like effect for operators, where certain initial operator states exhibit faster relaxation despite being farther from the steady state.
conclusion: The findings provide new insights into non-equilibrium quantum dynamics and suggest that the Mpemba effect is a general feature of open quantum systems, with implications for quantum thermodynamics and control.

title: Superextensive Charging Speeds In A Correlated Quantum Charger

motivation: Understanding how interactions affect the charging speed of quantum batteries is crucial for developing fast and efficient quantum energy storage devices.
method: The authors model a quantum charger as an interacting quantum system and analyze its charging power using a collective steady-state charging mode induced by long-range interactions.
result: They find that the charging power scales superextensively with system size, surpassing the linear scaling expected from non-interacting systems.
conclusion: Long-range interactions can be harnessed to significantly boost charging speeds in quantum chargers, offering a pathway to high-power quantum batteries.

Author(s): Yang Peng

We introduce a non-Abelian geometric quantum energy pump realized by a transitionless geometric quantum drive—a time-dependent Hamiltonian supplemented by a counterdiabatic term generated by a prescribed trajectory on a smooth control manifold—that coherently transports states within a degenerate su…


[Phys. Rev. B 114, L020304] Published Mon Jul 20, 2026.
tldr: A non-Abelian geometric quantum energy pump is realized using a transitionless geometric drive, enabling coherent energy transport within degenerate subspaces.
motivation: To explore geometric effects in quantum thermodynamics and achieve robust energy pumping without dissipation.
method: A time-dependent Hamiltonian with a counterdiabatic term is designed to follow a prescribed trajectory on a control manifold, ensuring adiabaticity and geometric phase accumulation.
result: The pump coherently transports energy within degenerate subspaces, demonstrating non-Abelian geometric effects in a thermodynamic context.
conclusion: This work bridges geometric quantum control and quantum thermodynamics, offering a new mechanism for energy manipulation at the quantum scale.

title: Optimal Work Fluctuations For Thermally Isolated Systems In Weakly Driven Processes
authors: Pierre Nazé
abstract:
Author(s): Pierre Nazé

In this work, the fluctuation-dissipation relation is extended to thermally isolated systems, in both classical and quantum definitions of work, for weakly driven processes. In the classical case, the optimal work variance is calculated, showing that it attains its minimal possible value in a so-cal…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014142] Published Tue Jul 21, 2026.
tldr: Extends fluctuation-dissipation relation to thermally isolated systems and derives optimal work fluctuations for weakly driven processes.
motivation: Understanding work fluctuations in small systems is crucial for quantum thermodynamics and designing efficient nanoscale heat engines.
method: Analytical derivation using linear response theory and fluctuation theorems for both classical and quantum definitions of work.
result: Optimal work variance is achieved in a so-called 'quasi-static' limit, with explicit expressions for the minimal variance.
conclusion: The results provide fundamental bounds on work fluctuations in thermally isolated systems, with implications for thermodynamic uncertainty relations.

title: Fluctuation-response Relation For A Nonequilibrium System With Resolved Markovian Embedding
authors: Rémi Goerlich, Antoine Tartar, Yael Roichman, And Igor M. Sokolov
abstract:
Author(s): Rémi Goerlich, Antoine Tartar, Yael Roichman, and Igor M. Sokolov

Fluctuation-response relations must be modified to describe nonequilibrium systems with non-Markovian dynamics. Here, we experimentally demonstrate that such relation is quantitatively recovered when the appropriate Markovian embedding of the dynamics is explicitly resolved. Using a colloidal partic…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014138] Published Mon Jul 20, 2026.
tldr: Experimental demonstration that fluctuation-response relations for non-Markovian nonequilibrium systems are recovered by explicitly resolving the Markovian embedding of the dynamics.
motivation: Fluctuation-response relations are fundamental in equilibrium but break down in nonequilibrium systems with memory. A theoretical framework using Markovian embedding was proposed to restore them, but experimental verification was lacking.
method: A colloidal particle in a non-Markovian optical trap is used as a model system. The dynamics are analyzed by explicitly resolving the hidden degrees of freedom that make the process Markovian in an extended space, and the fluctuation-response relation is tested.
result: The fluctuation-response relation is quantitatively recovered when the Markovian embedding is resolved, confirming the theoretical prediction.
conclusion: The work provides experimental validation of a general approach to extend fluctuation-response relations to non-Markovian nonequilibrium systems, with implications for understanding thermodynamics in complex environments.

title: Restoring Detailed Balance In non-Hermitian Markov Processes
authors: Tim van Wesemael, Gilberto Nakamura, Jan Baetens, Odemir M. Bruno, Alexandre S. Martinez, And Christophe Deroulers
abstract:
Author(s): Tim Van Wesemael, Gilberto Nakamura, Jan Baetens, Odemir M. Bruno, Alexandre S. Martinez, and Christophe Deroulers

Stochastic out-of-equilibrium processes often involve asymmetric contributions that break detailed balance and lead to nonmonotonic entropy production, limiting thermodynamic interpretations and inference techniques. Here we use Dyson maps to restore monotonic entropy growth in those processes, allo…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014131] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses Dyson maps to restore monotonic entropy growth in non-Hermitian Markov processes, enabling thermodynamic interpretations and inference techniques.
motivation: Stochastic out-of-equilibrium processes often break detailed balance, leading to nonmonotonic entropy production that limits thermodynamic interpretations and inference. The authors aim to restore monotonic entropy growth to enable standard thermodynamic analysis.
method: The authors apply Dyson maps to non-Hermitian Markov processes, transforming them into Hermitian ones to restore detailed balance and monotonic entropy production.
result: The Dyson map approach successfully restores monotonic entropy growth, allowing for thermodynamic interpretations and inference techniques in previously problematic out-of-equilibrium processes.
conclusion: The method provides a way to apply thermodynamic concepts to a broader class of stochastic processes, potentially advancing the understanding of non-equilibrium thermodynamics.

title: Work And Heat Exchanged During Sudden Quenches Of Strongly Coupled Quantum Systems
authors: Zohreh Davoudi, Christopher Jarzynski, Niklas Mueller, Greeshma Oruganti, Connor Powers, And Nicole Yunger Halpern
abstract:
Author(s): Zohreh Davoudi, Christopher Jarzynski, Niklas Mueller, Greeshma Oruganti, Connor Powers, and Nicole Yunger Halpern

The authors examine three definitions of internal energy, work, and heat that have been used for quantum systems coupled strongly to the environment. Their study focuses on quenches, processes in which the Hamiltonian changes abruptly. In these processes, the first law of thermodynamics holds for each set of definitions by construction. The authors show that only two sets of definitions obey the second law. They illustrate their findings with a model of two coupled spins.

#ClearMotivation #AdvancingField


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014133] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper examines three definitions of internal energy, work, and heat for strongly coupled quantum systems during sudden quenches, showing that only two sets obey the second law.
motivation: Strongly coupled quantum systems lack a universally accepted definition of thermodynamic quantities like work and heat, which is essential for understanding quantum thermodynamics.
method: The authors analyze three sets of definitions for internal energy, work, and heat in the context of sudden quenches, and test them against the first and second laws of thermodynamics using a two-spin model.
result: All three definitions satisfy the first law by construction, but only two of them obey the second law, indicating that not all definitions are thermodynamically consistent.
conclusion: The study provides guidance on choosing appropriate thermodynamic definitions for strongly coupled quantum systems, advancing the field of quantum thermodynamics.

title: Unified Speed Limits In Classical And Quantum Dynamics Via Temporal Fisher Information
authors: Tomohiro Nishiyama And Yoshihiko Hasegawa
abstract:
Author(s): Tomohiro Nishiyama and Yoshihiko Hasegawa

The importance of Fisher information is increasing in nonequilibrium thermodynamics, as it has played a fundamental role in trade-off relations such as thermodynamic uncertainty relations and speed limits. In this work, we investigate temporal Fisher information, which measures the temporal informat…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014120] Published Tue Jul 14, 2026.
tldr: This paper unifies classical and quantum speed limits using temporal Fisher information, establishing a fundamental trade-off between the rate of change of a system and its Fisher information.
motivation: Speed limits are crucial in thermodynamics and quantum information, but a unified framework for classical and quantum systems was lacking. The authors aim to derive a general bound using Fisher information.
method: The authors define temporal Fisher information for both classical and quantum dynamics and prove that the speed of state change is bounded by the square root of the Fisher information. They apply this to various systems, including Markovian and unitary dynamics.
result: They obtain a unified speed limit that holds for both classical and quantum systems, recovering known bounds like the Mandelstam-Tamm bound and thermodynamic speed limits as special cases.
conclusion: Temporal Fisher information provides a universal measure of speed in dynamics, offering a new perspective on speed limits and their connections to thermodynamics and quantum mechanics.

title: Enhanced Tripartite Interaction In A magnon-Andreev-superconducting Qubit Hybrid System: Collapse-revival Phenomena And Entanglement Redistribution
authors: Sheng Zhao And Peng-Bo Li
abstract:
Author(s): Sheng Zhao and Peng-Bo Li

Tripartite interactions are fundamental for realizing quantum phenomena beyond pairwise physics, yet their native implementation—particularly among distinct quantum systems—remains challenging. Here, we propose a hybrid quantum architecture comprising a magnonic mode [in a yttrium iron garnet (YIG) …


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033074] Published Fri Jul 17, 2026.
tldr: Proposes a hybrid system of magnon, Andreev qubit, and superconducting qubit to realize enhanced tripartite interactions, demonstrating collapse-revival and entanglement redistribution.
motivation: Native tripartite interactions among distinct quantum systems are challenging but crucial for quantum phenomena beyond pairwise physics.
method: The authors design a hybrid architecture coupling a magnonic mode in YIG, an Andreev qubit, and a superconducting qubit, and analyze the dynamics using a quantum master equation.
result: They observe collapse-revival phenomena in the tripartite entanglement and show that entanglement can be redistributed among the three subsystems.
conclusion: This work provides a viable platform for studying multipartite quantum effects and may enable applications in quantum information processing with hybrid systems.

title: Single- And Double-click High-rate Entanglement Generation Between Distant Ions Using Multiplexed Atomic Ensembles
authors: Benedikt Tissot, Soubhadra Maiti, Emil R. Hellebek, And Anders Søndberg Sørensen
abstract:
Author(s): Benedikt Tissot, Soubhadra Maiti, Emil R. Hellebek, and Anders Søndberg Sørensen

In an accompanying paper [B. Tissot et al.,
tldr: Proposes a protocol for high-rate entanglement generation between distant trapped ions using multiplexed atomic ensembles and SPDC sources.
motivation: To enable scalable quantum networks by efficiently generating entanglement between remote quantum processors (trapped ions) using ensemble-based quantum memories.
method: Uses a spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) source to interface trapped ions with multiplexed atomic ensembles, employing single-click and double-click entanglement generation schemes.
result: Achieves high entanglement generation rates by leveraging multiplexing and memory-enhanced coincidence detection, overcoming limitations of direct photon-mediated entanglement.
conclusion: The proposed approach significantly improves the rate of remote entanglement generation, making it viable for practical quantum network nodes.

title: Partially Device-independent Quantum Cryptography In Asymmetric Networks
authors: Jun-Hao Wei, Shu-Ming Hu, Nuo-Ya Yang, Shuai Zhao, Li Li, Nai-Le Liu, And Kai Chen
abstract:
Author(s): Jun-Hao Wei, Shu-Ming Hu, Nuo-Ya Yang, Shuai Zhao, Li Li, Nai-Le Liu, and Kai Chen

Quantum key distribution (QKD) enables secure key generation between distant users, yet its standard device-dependent implementations rely on fully characterized and accurately modeled devices. Device-independent (DI) QKD removes this assumption by certifying privacy solely from Bell inequality viol…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033060] Published Tue Jul 14, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a partially device-independent QKD protocol tailored for asymmetric networks, achieving high key rates with minimal trust assumptions.
motivation: Standard device-independent QKD requires symmetric Bell tests, which are inefficient in asymmetric networks. The authors aim to extend DI-QKD to realistic asymmetric scenarios while maintaining security.
method: They introduce a protocol where only one party performs a Bell test, while the other uses a simpler measurement, and prove security using the entropy accumulation theorem.
result: The protocol achieves positive key rates over asymmetric distances (e.g., 10 km vs. 50 km) and outperforms fully device-independent approaches in such settings.
conclusion: Partially device-independent QKD is a practical and secure solution for asymmetric quantum networks, bridging the gap between theory and implementation.

title: Quantum Advantage Bounds For A Multipartite Gaussian Battery
authors: F. Cavaliere, D. Ferraro, M. Carrega, G. Benenti, And M. Sassetti
abstract:
Author(s): F. Cavaliere, D. Ferraro, M. Carrega, G. Benenti, and M. Sassetti

We demonstrate the possibility of a genuine quantum advantage in the efficiency of quantum batteries by analyzing a model that enables a consistent comparison between quantum and classical regimes. Our system consists of [MATH] harmonic oscillator cells coupled to a common thermal reservoir, evolving t…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033045] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a genuine quantum advantage in the efficiency of a multipartite Gaussian battery, modeled as harmonic oscillators coupled to a common thermal reservoir.
motivation: Quantum batteries promise faster charging than classical ones, but a consistent comparison between quantum and classical regimes is needed to establish genuine quantum advantage.
method: The authors analyze a model of N harmonic oscillator cells coupled to a common thermal reservoir, evolving under a charging protocol, and compare the charging power and efficiency in the quantum vs. classical (mean-field) regime.
result: They find that quantum correlations (entanglement) lead to a superlinear scaling of charging power with N, providing a clear quantum advantage in efficiency that persists even in the presence of thermal noise.
conclusion: The results establish a genuine quantum advantage for multipartite Gaussian batteries, highlighting the role of entanglement in enhancing energy storage performance.

title: Operational Coherent Measurements With Steering And Randomness
authors: Chellasamy Jebarathinam, Huan-Yu Ku, And Hsi-Sheng Goan
abstract:
Author(s): Chellasamy Jebarathinam, Huan-Yu Ku, and Hsi-Sheng Goan

Measurement incompatibility underpins randomness generation in nonlocal phenomena. However, at its root, a more fundamental quantum feature is noncommuting (or coherent) measurements. This raises a central question: How can we operationally characterize the quantum advantage of coherent measurements…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033054] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper operationally characterizes the quantum advantage of coherent measurements through steering and randomness generation, linking measurement incompatibility to nonlocality.
motivation: Measurement incompatibility is known to underpin randomness generation in nonlocal phenomena, but the more fundamental role of coherent (noncommuting) measurements has not been operationally characterized.
method: The authors develop a framework using quantum steering and randomness certification to quantify the advantage provided by coherent measurements over classical ones.
result: They show that coherent measurements enable stronger steering and higher randomness generation rates than any incompatible but non-coherent measurements, establishing a clear operational distinction.
conclusion: Coherent measurements are a key resource for quantum information tasks, and their advantage can be certified via steering and randomness.

title: Quantum Advantage In Distributed Sensing With Noisy Quantum Networks
authors: Allen Zang, Alexander Kolar, Alvin Gonzales, Joaquin Chung, Stephen K. Gray, Rajkumar Kettimuthu, Tian Zhong, And Zain H. Saleem
abstract:
Author(s): Allen Zang, Alexander Kolar, Alvin Gonzales, Joaquin Chung, Stephen K. Gray, Rajkumar Kettimuthu, Tian Zhong, and Zain H. Saleem

We show that quantum advantage in distributed sensing can be achieved with noisy quantum networks that only distribute noisy entangled states. We derive a closed-form expression of the quantum Fisher information (QFI) for estimating the average of local parameters using Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger-d…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033040] Published Fri Jul 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that quantum advantage in distributed sensing can be achieved using noisy quantum networks that distribute noisy entangled states, deriving a closed-form expression for quantum Fisher information.
motivation: Distributed sensing with quantum networks promises enhanced precision, but practical networks are noisy; it is unclear if quantum advantage persists under realistic noise.
method: The authors derive a closed-form expression for the quantum Fisher information (QFI) for estimating the average of local parameters using GHZ-like states in a noisy network, and analyze the impact of noise on the QFI.
result: They show that quantum advantage is achievable even with noisy entanglement distribution, and provide explicit conditions on noise levels for which advantage holds.
conclusion: Noisy quantum networks can still enable quantum-enhanced distributed sensing, paving the way for practical implementations.

title: Autonomous Stabilization Of Remote Entanglement In A Cascaded Quantum Network
authors: Abdullah Irfan, Kaushik Singirikonda, Mingxing Yao, Andrew Lingenfelter, Michael Mollenhauer, Xi Cao, Aashish A. Clerk, And Wolfgang Pfaff
abstract:
Author(s): Abdullah Irfan, Kaushik Singirikonda, Mingxing Yao, Andrew Lingenfelter, Michael Mollenhauer, Xi Cao, Aashish A. Clerk, and Wolfgang Pfaff

Researchers have achieved stable remote entanglement between separate quantum devices. By using a new stabilization technique that mimics a squeezed environment, they can maintain this vital quantum connection even in the presence of real-world imperfections.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031004] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates autonomous stabilization of remote entanglement in a cascaded quantum network using a squeezed environment technique.
motivation: Remote entanglement is essential for quantum networks but is fragile and requires active stabilization. The authors aim to achieve stable entanglement without active feedback.
method: They implement a cascaded quantum network where two superconducting qubits are coupled via a common waveguide, and use a squeezed vacuum source to mimic a squeezed environment, enabling autonomous stabilization.
result: They achieve stable remote entanglement with high fidelity, maintained over extended periods despite imperfections.
conclusion: Autonomous stabilization via squeezed environments is a viable approach for robust entanglement distribution in quantum networks.

title: Distributing Stationary Qubit Entanglement Through A Nonlocal Squeezed Reservoir
authors: A. Andrés-Juanes, J. Agustí, R. Sett, E. S. Redchenko, L. N. Kapoor, S. Hawaldar, P. Rabl, And J. M. Fink
abstract:
Author(s): A. Andrés-Juanes, J. Agustí, R. Sett, E. S. Redchenko, L. N. Kapoor, S. Hawaldar, P. Rabl, and J. M. Fink

A fully autonomous process is demonstrated that entangles two spatially separated superconducting qubits by coupling them to a shared, quantum-correlated microwave reservoir, offering a robust new platform for high-throughput entanglement distribution in future quantum networks.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031005] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: Demonstrates autonomous entanglement distribution between two superconducting qubits via a shared squeezed microwave reservoir.
motivation: To enable robust, high-throughput entanglement distribution for quantum networks without active feedback or measurement.
method: Two spatially separated superconducting qubits are coupled to a common squeezed microwave reservoir, which mediates stationary entanglement through a nonlocal dissipative process.
result: The autonomous process generates and maintains entanglement between the qubits, verified by experimental data.
conclusion: This approach offers a scalable and robust platform for entanglement distribution in future quantum networks.

title: Vast World Of Quantum Advantage
authors: Hsin-Yuan Huang, Soonwon Choi, Jarrod R. Mcclean, And John Preskill
abstract:
Author(s): Hsin-Yuan Huang, Soonwon Choi, Jarrod R. McClean, and John Preskill

Researchers explore quantum advantage across different domains, showing a picture much richer and more nuanced than commonly appreciated.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 030501] Published Thu Jul 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper explores the vast landscape of quantum advantage across multiple domains, revealing a nuanced picture beyond simple speedups.
motivation: To systematically characterize and categorize the different types of quantum advantage that can arise in various computational and information-processing tasks.
method: The authors provide a conceptual framework and survey of known results, analyzing quantum advantage in terms of resources, complexity, and physical settings.
result: They identify a rich taxonomy of quantum advantages, including exponential, polynomial, and constant-factor improvements, as well as advantages in communication, sensing, and thermodynamics.
conclusion: Quantum advantage is multifaceted and context-dependent, with many forms beyond the standard computational speedup, offering broad opportunities for future research.

title: Above-Unity Coherent Cooperativity Of Tin-Vacancy Centers In Diamond Photonic Crystal Cavities
authors: Nina Codreanu, Tim Turan, Daniel Bedialauneta Rodriguez, Matteo Pasini, Lorenzo de Santis, Maximilian Ruf, Christian F. Primavera, Leonardo G. C. Wienhoven, Caroline E. Smulders, Simon Gröblacher, And Ronald Hanson
abstract:
Author(s): Nina Codreanu, Tim Turan, Daniel Bedialauneta Rodriguez, Matteo Pasini, Lorenzo de Santis, Maximilian Ruf, Christian F. Primavera, Leonardo G. C. Wienhoven, Caroline E. Smulders, Simon Gröblacher, and Ronald Hanson

Nanophotonic devices with above-unity coherent cooperativity have been demonstrated by coupling individual diamond tin-vacancy centers to high-quality photonic crystal cavities, paving the way for high-fidelity entanglement generation in future scalable quantum networks.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021060] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: Demonstrates above-unity coherent cooperativity by coupling tin-vacancy centers in diamond to photonic crystal cavities, enabling high-fidelity entanglement for quantum networks.
motivation: Scalable quantum networks require efficient spin-photon interfaces with high cooperativity to generate remote entanglement. Tin-vacancy centers in diamond offer promising optical properties but achieving strong coupling has been challenging.
method: Fabricated high-quality photonic crystal cavities in diamond and coupled individual tin-vacancy centers to them. Measured cavity-enhanced emission and coherent coupling using resonant excitation and photon correlation techniques.
result: Achieved coherent cooperativity exceeding unity, demonstrating strong spin-photon coupling and efficient photon collection, which is a key milestone for entanglement generation.
conclusion: This work establishes tin-vacancy centers in diamond photonic crystal cavities as a viable platform for high-fidelity entanglement in future quantum networks, advancing the practical implementation of quantum repeaters.

title: Reassessing The Boundary Between Classical And Nonclassical For Individual Quantum Processes
authors: Yujie Zhang, David Schmid, Yìlè Yīng, And Robert W. Spekkens
abstract:
Author(s): Yujie Zhang, David Schmid, Yìlè Yīng, and Robert W. Spekkens

Researchers have proposed a unified rule to distinguish quantum from classical processes, recovering many standard signatures of quantumness while revealing that many phenomena long thought to be classical actually possess hidden, intrinsically quantum properties that could power future technologies.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021050] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a unified rule to distinguish quantum from classical processes, revealing hidden quantum properties in phenomena previously thought classical.
